html:
Bruges is a city in Flanders, now in Belgium, that from the late 13th century to about 1500 was the main market of northern Europe, where Italian galleys met the ships of the Hanseatic League.

The city grew on the cloth trade of Flanders, which used wool from England. A storm in 1134 opened a channel, the Zwin, that linked it to the sea. In 1277 the first Genoese galleys arrived from the Mediterranean, and the Venetian fleets soon followed. Merchants of many nations kept houses there: Italians, Castilians, Germans and English. The Hansa had its main western office in Bruges. Meetings of traders at the house of the Van der Beurse family gave the word "bourse" for an exchange.

The historian Fernand Braudel saw Bruges as the northern pole of a European economy that had not yet found one centre, before Venice and then Antwerp took the lead. Under the dukes of Burgundy in the 15th century it was also a centre of art, home to Jan van Eyck. As the Zwin silted up and trade moved to Antwerp, Bruges declined after about 1500.
sum: Bruges is a city in Flanders, now in Belgium, that from the late 13th century to about 1500 was the main market of northern Europe, where Italian galleys met the ships of the Hanseatic League.
